summary: Updates the POP3 mailbox protocol from RFC 1939 with a way for servers to announce which optional commands and extensions they support. A client can ask and then use only what is available. It is a proposed standard and was itself updated by RFC 5034.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2449 lets a POP3 client ask a server which optional commands and behaviors it supports. The server responds with a capability list so the client can adapt without probing.

subtitle: A way for POP3 servers to announce optional commands and behavior before clients use them.

tldr.problem: POP3 servers may support optional commands or behaviors, but clients had no standard way to learn about them without trying commands or using manual settings.
tldr.mechanism: The CAPA command lists server capabilities. The RFC also defines initial capability names, extended response codes, and a formal command and response grammar.
tldr.outcome: Clients can adapt to server support while POP3 remains a simple download-and-delete protocol. RFC 2449 updates RFC 1939 and is itself updated by RFC 5034.

today: RFC 2449 is a Proposed Standard published in November 1998 and updates RFC 1939. It was updated by RFC 5034 and has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why POP3 Announces Capabilities
sections.content:
POP3 has optional commands and extensions, but earlier protocol rules did not provide a general way for a server to advertise them. Clients often had to probe or rely on manual settings.

RFC 2449 updates RFC 1939 with the CAPA command, an initial set of capabilities, extended response codes, and a formal grammar. An IESG note emphasizes that POP3 should remain simple and points to IMAP for more complicated mail access.
sections.plainLanguage: Before this extension, a client often had to guess which POP3 features a server supported. CAPA lets the server list its available features.

sections.title: Command Grammar and Lengths
sections.content:
The RFC specifies command and response forms using ABNF. A command has a three- or four-character keyword followed by optional space-separated parameters.

A command can be up to 255 octets, including its terminating CRLF. CAPA-capable servers MUST accept that length and the largest command length required by any capability they support. The first response line and each capability line can be up to 512 octets.
sections.plainLanguage: The grammar defines how POP3 commands and responses are written. CAPA-capable servers accept commands up to 255 octets and capability lines up to 512 octets.

sections.title: The CAPA Command
sections.content:
CAPA takes no arguments and is available in the AUTHORIZATION and TRANSACTION states. An -ERR response means the server does not implement CAPA, so the client must use its earlier discovery method.

An +OK response is followed by one capability per line, optionally with parameters. The list ends with a line containing only a period. Each capability description states in which states it is announced and where its commands are valid.

If authentication negotiates an integrity-protection layer, the client SHOULD issue CAPA again after authentication to check for down-negotiation attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: The client sends CAPA, and the server returns one capability on each line. A line containing only a period marks the end of the list.

sections.title: The Initial Capability Set
sections.content:
The RFC defines nine initial capabilities: TOP, USER, SASL, RESP-CODES, LOGIN-DELAY, PIPELINING, EXPIRE, UIDL, and IMPLEMENTATION. Some announce optional commands; others describe authentication methods or server behavior.

LOGIN-DELAY states the minimum time between logins. EXPIRE states a minimum message-retention period or NEVER; EXPIRE 0 means the client may not leave mail on the server. PIPELINING permits several commands to be outstanding, with server processing and replies kept in order.

IMPLEMENTATION identifies the server, but clients MUST NOT change their behavior based on that string. APOP is not a capability because its challenge appears in the greeting.
sections.plainLanguage: The initial list covers optional commands, authentication, login timing, message retention, and pipelining. Clients use these values to follow server policy and choose supported operations.

sections.title: Extended Response Codes
sections.content:
POP3 normally reports success or failure, but clients may need to distinguish why a command failed. A server that advertises RESP-CODES can put a machine-readable code in square brackets at the start of response text.

Codes are case-insensitive and may have slash-separated levels of detail. Clients MUST ignore unknown details so that future specifications can add them.

The initial codes are LOGIN-DELAY, for a login attempt made too soon, and IN-USE, for successful authentication when the maildrop is already in use.
sections.plainLanguage: A response code gives a client more detail than a simple success or failure. Clients must ignore code details they do not recognize.

sections.title: Security and Future Extensions
sections.content:
A capability list can reveal which authentication mechanisms a server supports, which may help an attacker assess possible attacks. It can also help a client choose a stronger available method.

LOGIN-DELAY in response to USER can reveal that a named account exists. The RFC strongly recommends that servers avoid this response unless names are not secret, access is restricted, or the server can verify the connection is from the same user.

The RFC discourages extensions that make POP3 depart from its download-and-delete purpose. Clients MUST NOT require extensions for basic operation, apart from authentication commands.
sections.plainLanguage: Capability information can help clients choose authentication, but can also reveal server details. A server should avoid confirming an account's existence in response to USER.
